groups.title: Authentication Concepts
groups.question: Your JAMstack site needs users to log in with Google and access a members-only area. Explain the login flow and how you would keep users signed in.

followUps.OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect flows expla: How do OAuth and OpenID Connect differ, and which flow should a web app use?
followUps.JWT structure, signing, and verification: How is a JWT verified without looking anything up?
followUps.Session cookies versus token-based authe: Why are session cookies often a better default for web apps than tokens in storage?

evidence.text: OAuth lets an app get permission to act for the user through an identity provider.
OpenID Connect adds a standard way to learn who the user is.
The authorization code flow with PKCE is the recommended flow for web apps.

notEnough: Only saying OAuth is for login.

evidence.text: A JWT has a header, a payload of claims and a signature.
The server checks the signature with a secret or public key.
If the signature and expiry are valid, no session lookup is needed.

misconceptions.text: Says a JWT's payload is encrypted.

evidence.text: A session cookie holds an id that the server looks up.
HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by scripts, which protects against XSS theft.
Self-contained tokens avoid lookups but are harder to revoke and risky to store in the browser.

notEnough: Only saying cookies are more secure.

groups.title: Roles and Access Control
groups.question: Members can read premium articles, admins can edit them, and your serverless functions serve the article data. Explain how you would control access.

followUps.Role-based access control and gated cont: How would you restrict content by role?
followUps.Protecting serverless API routes from un: Why must every serverless function check the token itself?

evidence.text: Users are given roles like admin or member.
Each protected route or resource checks the role before allowing access.
Roles can be stored as claims in the token so checks do not need a database lookup.
Functions are stateless and anyone can call them directly.
Each one must verify the token on every request.
Requests without a valid token are rejected with 401.

groups.title: Auth Providers and SDKs
groups.question: You are choosing between NextAuth and Netlify Identity to add login to your site. Explain how each is set up.

followUps.NextAuth.js setup with GitHub and Google: What do you need to set up GitHub login with NextAuth?
followUps.Netlify Identity for zero-config JAMstac: What does Netlify Identity give you without backend code?

evidence.text: NextAuth is added as a route handler in the Next.js app.
You register an OAuth app with GitHub to get a client id and secret.
Those credentials are stored as environment variables.
It provides sign-up, login and token issuing.
A widget handles the login UI.
Serverless functions on Netlify can read the logged-in user from the request.

groups.title: Login Flows and Route Protection
groups.question: You are building login and sign-up forms and need to keep signed-out users away from /account. Explain how you would build the forms and protect the route.

followUps.Building login and signup forms with val: Why validate login forms on both the client and the server?

evidence.text: The form sends credentials to an auth endpoint.
Client-side checks give quick feedback on mistakes.
The server must validate again because client checks can be bypassed.

notEnough: Only saying you validate the form.

evidence.text: Middleware runs before matched routes are rendered.
It checks for a valid session cookie or token.
If there is none, it redirects to the login page.
